units.title: Make surveys comparable
units.lesson: Dental surveys need consistent measurement criteria. WHO's survey manual supports standardization so results can be compared. Record what was measured, in whom and when.
units.question: Which approach best supports comparing two dental surveys?
choices: Change the case definition between surveys
Use the same defined measurement criteria
units.explanation: Comparable measurement requires consistent criteria and clear context.

units.title: Count people, then check the denominator
units.lesson: A count alone does not describe the proportion affected. Relate cases to the population from which they arose. Use matching persons, place and time.
units.question: Survey A records 20 affected people among 100 examined; B records 20 among 200. Which has the larger affected proportion?
choices: They must be equal because counts match
units.explanation: A: 20%. B: 10%. Equal counts can represent different proportions.

units.title: Point prevalence: who has the condition now?
units.lesson: Point prevalence describes existing cases at a specified time. Divide affected people by all people examined at that time. A one-day survey does not by itself identify when each condition began.
units.question: In a fictional one-day dental survey, 30 of 150 examined people meet the stated condition definition. What is the prevalence?
units.explanation: 30/150 × 100 = 20%. Include all 150 examined people, not just unaffected people.
rationales: 5 is the inverse ratio, not the percentage.

units.title: Incidence: identify new cases over time
units.lesson: Incidence concerns new cases beginning during a defined period. State the observation period and population at risk. Existing cases on a survey date alone do not establish incidence.
units.question: Which information distinguishes incidence from a snapshot of existing cases?
choices: The total number of clinic chairs
New cases arising during a defined follow-up period
Only the number of existing cases today
units.hint: Look for onset and elapsed time.
units.explanation: Incidence requires identifying new cases within the stated period.
rationales: Clinic capacity is not disease occurrence.
New cases and an observation period are central.
Existing cases alone describe a prevalence snapshot.

units.title: Apply it: a changed definition
units.lesson: Use the measurement principle in a new situation.
units.question: Two surveys report different affected percentages but use different case definitions. What should you check before concluding that disease frequency changed?
choices: Which percentage has more decimal places
Whether both reports have colourful charts
units.hint: Check the method before comparing the result.
units.explanation: A definition change may alter who is counted. Establish comparability first.
rationales: Extra decimals do not repair incompatible criteria.
Presentation style does not establish comparability.

units.title: Apply it: equal percentages
units.lesson: Work from the counts rather than memorising the previous answer.
units.question: One fictional survey has 12 affected among 60 people; another has 30 among 150. Which statement is correct?
units.explanation: 12/60 = 30/150 = 0.20. The raw counts differ, but the proportions match.

units.title: Apply it: a fresh survey
units.lesson: Now use a different numerator and denominator.
units.question: On one stated survey date, 36 of 120 examined people meet a fictional dental condition definition. What proportion is affected?
units.explanation: 36/120 × 100 = 30%. A case count is not automatically a percentage.
rationales: 36 is the count, not the percentage.

units.title: Apply it: incidence proportion
units.lesson: For a closed cohort initially free of a condition, incidence proportion uses new cases divided by the initial at-risk population. This is a risk over a period, not a person-time incidence rate.
units.question: All 60 initially condition-free people complete one year of follow-up; 6 develop the fictional condition. What is the one-year incidence proportion?
units.hint: Use new cases ÷ initially at risk.
units.explanation: 6/60 × 100 = 10% over one year. Complete follow-up is an explicit assumption.
